meta.subtitle: Internally managed sustainable-infrastructure investor with an origination inflection and a 4.67% yield

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate HA Sustainable Infrastructure Capital a BUY with a target range of $38 to $50 against a current price of $36.25. Our probability-weighted fair value is about $41, an expected upside near 14%, with a bear-case downside around 25% and a reward/risk of roughly 0.54x. The case is an origination inflection: the company closed approximately $1.1 billion of transactions in Q2'26 against $189 million a year earlier, its pipeline exceeds $6.5 billion, and the shares yield 4.67%. This is a specialty-finance company, so its income statement has no gross margin, operating income or EBITDA lines, and the 62.5x trailing P/E reflects volatile gain-on-sale earnings rather than the forward earning power implied by the 12.0x next-twelve-months multiple. We hold the conviction to a moderate BUY because results are sensitive to interest rates, which the 10-Q's discussion of factors affecting operating results cites, and to clean-energy policy, which the 10-K flags as able to reduce demand for the projects the company finances.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: HA Sustainable Infrastructure Capital, founded in 1981 and known as Hannon Armstrong until a June 2024 name change, invests in energy-efficiency, renewable-energy and other sustainable-infrastructure assets. It is internally managed by a team of over 170 investment, operating and technical professionals and invests across three markets: Behind-the-Meter, Grid-Connected, and Fuels, Transport and Nature. The company earns net investment income from its portfolio, residual income from securitization and co-investment structures, and asset-management and gain-on-sale fees. As of June 30, 2026 it reported total Managed Assets of $17.6 billion and a balance-sheet Portfolio of approximately $8.2 billion. FY25 revenue was $400.5 million, up 4.4%, and net income was $184.5 million.

thesis.label: BUY
thesis.body: The thesis is an origination inflection funding a covered dividend. The company completed approximately $1.1 billion of transactions in Q2'26, well above the $189 million of the year-earlier quarter, and its pipeline exceeds $6.5 billion. The shares yield 4.67% and trade at 12.0x next-twelve-months earnings, a discount to the growth on offer if origination converts. The offset is sensitivity to two external forces: the cost of the debt the company raises to invest, and government policy on renewable energy. Our BUY reflects an expected upside near 14% against a bear-case downside near 25%, a reward/risk of about 0.54x, so it is a moderate-conviction position where the yield provides some support while the macro and policy risks are worked through.

catalysts: Origination growth: approximately $1.7 billion of transactions closed in the first six months of 2026 against $894 million a year earlier, feeding future net investment income.
That pipeline is split roughly 35% Behind-the-Meter, 51% Grid-Connected and 8% Fuels, Transport and Nature, weighted toward utility-scale renewables.
Capital-light fee income from the KKR co-investment vehicle and approximately $7.4 billion of assets managed in securitization trusts.
A consensus target of $49.80, about 37% above the current price, with 13 of 16 analysts rating the shares Buy.
Consensus EPS estimates of $3.02 for FY26E, above the $1.41 reported for FY25.
risks: Clean-energy policy: the 10-K warns that reductions to net-metering rules, government subsidies or FERC-regulated market structures could cut demand for the projects the company finances.
Commodity substitution: low natural-gas prices can reduce the demand for, and the contracted price of, the renewable-energy projects in the portfolio.
Interest-rate and cost-of-capital risk, since the company funds investments with a mix of secured and unsecured, fixed- and floating-rate debt and equity.
Earnings volatility: gain-on-sale and securitization income is lumpy, which is why the trailing P/E and forward EPS estimates move sharply.
Portfolio credit risk across more than 600 assets whose off-takers include utilities, building owners and industrial counterparties.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: As a specialty-finance company, the income statement carries no gross margin, operating-income or EBITDA line; the Facts block shows these as not applicable. FY25 revenue was $400.5 million, up 4.4%, and Q2'26 revenue was $120.8 million, up 41.0% year over year. FY25 net income was $184.5 million and diluted EPS was $1.41, a trailing net margin of 18.6%. Reported revenue combines net investment income, residual securitization income, and asset-management and gain-on-sale fees, so it is not comparable to a product company's sales. The FY26E consensus revenue estimate of $108.5 million sits far below the FY25 reported figure; we flag that discontinuity rather than explain it, and judge the trajectory on EPS, origination volume and the dividend rather than on the revenue line. Consensus EPS estimates are $3.02 for FY26E and $2.21 for FY27E, a spread that reflects the lumpiness of gain-on-sale income.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: Total equity grew to $2.7 billion at FY25 from $1.6 billion in FY21. Against that equity the company holds an approximately $8.2 billion balance-sheet Portfolio, so it is levered in the way a finance company is, funding assets with a mix of secured and unsecured, fixed- and floating-rate debt, equity, and off-balance-sheet securitization and co-investment structures. The Facts block reports FY25 total debt of $225.2 million and net debt of $115 million; these figures capture only part of that financing stack and understate the leverage implied by that Portfolio against the equity base, so we do not lean on them. The Portfolio's weighted-average remaining life of about 16 years matches long-dated liabilities to long-dated recurring cash flows.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Operating cash flow was about $0.2 billion in FY25. The Facts block shows no capital-expenditure, free-cash-flow or buyback lines, which is expected for a finance company whose cash generation runs through investment and financing activity rather than operating capex. FY25 dividends paid were $209.8 million, and the shares yield 4.67%. The dividend is funded from the recurring net investment income and fee streams the company describes, but its coverage depends on continued origination and on access to the debt and equity markets that fund new investments.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: The shares trade at 62.5x trailing earnings, 10.1x sales and 12.0x next-twelve-months earnings, rising to 16.4x on the FY27E EPS estimate. The trailing multiple is not a useful anchor here because reported EPS is depressed and volatile from gain-on-sale timing; the forward multiple and the 4.67% dividend yield are the better guides. No peer multiple set was available in this pack, so we value the company against its own forward earnings, its dividend and the $8.2 billion Portfolio and $17.6 billion of Managed Assets behind it. Our scenarios turn on whether the origination inflection sustains and on how interest rates and clean-energy policy evolve.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Origination stays near the Q2'26 pace, the pipeline converts, interest rates ease the cost of capital, and clean-energy policy stabilizes, letting the multiple re-rate toward the consensus view. Implied price near $53, above the $49.80 consensus target and toward the $60.00 top of the analyst range.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Origination growth moderates from the Q2'26 rate but stays healthy, the dividend holds, and the forward multiple expands only modestly from 12.0x as rates and policy remain uncertain. Implied price about $42, below the consensus target.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: A rollback of net-metering or government subsidies, or a higher-for-longer cost of capital, slows origination and pressures portfolio returns, and the shares de-rate toward their 52-week low. Implied price near $27, roughly 25% below the current $36.25 and close to the $27.28 low of the range.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: Weighting the Bull at 27%, the Base at 48% and the Bear at 25% gives a fair value of about $41, an expected upside near 14% and a bear-case downside of roughly 25%, for a reward/risk of about 0.54x. The reward/risk is thin, which is why this is a moderate BUY rather than a high-conviction one. The dividend yield cushions the downside, but the Bear is a real scenario: the company's returns depend on external policy and rate conditions it does not control, and a deterioration in both at once is what takes the shares back toward their 52-week low.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The company reports as a single segment. Its approximately $8.2 billion Portfolio as of June 30, 2026 comprised roughly $4.1 billion of Behind-the-Meter assets, $2.6 billion of Grid-Connected assets and $1.5 billion of Fuels, Transport and Nature assets. By instrument, approximately 56% was equity-method investments in renewable-energy projects, 34% fixed-rate receivables and debt securities, 6% floating-rate receivables and 4% real estate and other assets. The Portfolio held over 600 transactions with an average size of about $12 million and a weighted-average remaining life of roughly 16 years, and sits within $17.6 billion of total Managed Assets.

moatFactors.name: Programmatic client relationships
moatFactors.body: Long-standing, programmatic relationships with leading U.S. clean-energy developers, utilities and energy-service companies generate recurring, repeatable investment and fee opportunities, which is the company's main source of proprietary deal flow and origination scale.

moatFactors.name: Internally managed cost structure
moatFactors.body: Being internally managed by a team of over 170 professionals avoids the external-manager fee drag common to comparable investment vehicles and aligns the cost base with the portfolio it runs.

moatFactors.name: Scale and co-investment structures
moatFactors.body: The Managed Assets base, the KKR co-investment vehicle and roughly $7.4 billion of securitized assets let the company earn fees on capital it does not fund directly, extending its reach beyond its own balance sheet.

moatFactors.name: Policy and rate dependence
moatFactors.body: Returns depend on renewable-energy economics that the 10-K ties to net-metering rules, government subsidies, FERC policy and commodity prices, so the moat is exposed to external forces the company cannot control.

businessMoat.durability: The recurring, contracted nature of the cash flows supports durability: the Portfolio's weighted-average life is about 16 years, off-takers are described as creditworthy and incentivized, and the investment criteria favor proven technologies. The offset is that the demand for new investment, and the value of existing assets, both hinge on clean-energy policy and the cost of capital. Durability is therefore real for the long-dated assets already on the books but conditional for the growth that the valuation partly assumes.

points: The origination inflection cited earlier converts to future net investment income as new transactions fund and season, so recent volume supports revenue beyond the current period.
The pipeline skews toward Grid-Connected utility-scale projects, which are larger than distributed Behind-the-Meter deals and shape the mix of future Portfolio additions.
The KKR co-investment vehicle and further co-investment structures expand the investments the company can make without funding them entirely on balance sheet.
Managed Assets of $17.6 billion provide a growing base of fee-generating and residual income alongside net investment income.
Management identifies markets beyond its three traditional ones as additional sources of investment aligned with its strategy.

management.leadership: The company is internally managed. Per the 2026 proxy, the named executive officers are Jeffrey A. Lipson, Director, Chief Executive Officer and President; Charles W. Melko, Senior Managing Director and Chief Financial Officer; Marc T. Pangburn, Senior Managing Director and Chief Revenue and Strategy Officer; Steven L. Chuslo, Executive Vice President and Chief Legal Officer; Nitya Gopalakrishnan, Senior Managing Director and Chief Operating Officer; and Susan D. Nickey, Senior Managing Director and Chief Client Officer. The team emphasizes attractive risk-adjusted returns that exceed the cost of capital.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation centers on funding new investments and paying the dividend. FY25 dividends paid were $209.8 million, supporting the 4.67% yield. The company funds its Portfolio through a mix of cash, secured and unsecured debt, equity, securitizations and co-investment structures, and manages interest-rate risk with hedging including interest-rate swaps. Investing more than 30% of equity capital in any single investment requires approval of a majority of independent directors, a stated discipline on concentration.
management.governance: The 2026 proxy reports that eight of ten director nominees are independent under NYSE standards: Lizabeth Ardisana, Clarence Armbrister, Teresa Brenner, Nancy Floyd, Steven Osgood, Kimberly Reed, Laura Schulte and Barry Welch. Teresa Brenner serves as Lead Independent Director, and the Audit, Compensation, Nominating/Governance and Finance/Risk committees are composed solely of independent directors. The company changed its name from Hannon Armstrong to HA Sustainable Infrastructure Capital in June 2024. There is no familial relationship among directors or executive officers.
management.insiderOwnership: As of the April 6, 2026 Record Date, all directors and executive officers as a group held 2,836,898 shares, or 2.2%, of the 131,387,206 shares of common stock and OP units then outstanding. Jeffrey W. Eckel held 1,011,994 shares and chief executive Jeffrey A. Lipson held 540,015. Institutional holders include BlackRock at 14.6%, Wellington Management at 10.3% and T. Rowe Price at 5.1%. Insider ownership is modest in percentage terms.

idiosyncratic: Clean-energy policy dependence: the 10-K warns that changes to net-metering rules, reductions in government subsidies or FERC-driven market changes could reduce demand for the projects the company finances and the returns on existing assets.
Interest-rate and cost-of-capital risk: because the company borrows to invest, a higher-for-longer rate environment raises funding costs and can compress the spread it earns over its cost of capital.
Earnings and dividend volatility: gain-on-sale and securitization income is lumpy, and continued dividend coverage depends on origination volume and access to capital markets.
Commodity substitution: because low natural-gas prices weaken renewable-project economics, a sustained decline could slow new business origination and mark down assets already held.

Credit concentration and complexity: the Portfolio spans over 600 assets across equity-method, receivable, debt-security and real-estate structures whose valuation relies on complex, judgment-heavy accounting.
risks.systemic: The company sits at the intersection of the capital markets and government energy policy. A broad rise in interest rates would raise its funding costs and pressure the value of long-dated assets, while a shift in federal or state policy away from supporting renewable energy would slow origination and could impair returns. Access to debt and equity markets is itself a systemic dependency: the model requires continual external financing to grow the Portfolio, so a capital-markets freeze would constrain both growth and the dividend.

body: We rate HA Sustainable Infrastructure Capital a BUY with a $38 to $50 target range around a probability-weighted fair value of about $41, an expected upside near 14% and a reward/risk of roughly 0.54x. The origination inflection is real and the pipeline is deep, the dividend yield pays investors to wait, and the book is backed by a large Managed Assets base of long-dated, contracted cash flows.

This is a moderate-conviction call rather than a strong one because the return depends on forces the company does not control. Interest rates set its cost of capital, which the 10-Q lists among the factors affecting operating results, while clean-energy policy, which the 10-K flags as able to reduce demand for what the company finances, drives origination. Reported earnings are volatile from gain-on-sale timing, and the summary balance-sheet debt figures understate a finance company's true leverage. Our Bear, about 25% below the current price and near the 52-week low, is the case where rates stay high and policy turns against renewables at the same time. We would prefer to accumulate toward the low end of our range.
